sections.authorBiography: O. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter, born on 11 September 1862 in Greensboro, North Carolina. He trained as a pharmacist, moved to Texas, and worked as a draftsman, bank teller and humorous journalist. Convicted of embezzling from the Austin bank where he had worked (he maintained his innocence), he served about three years in the Ohio Penitentiary (1898–1901), where he began publishing stories as O. Henry. In New York he wrote a story a week for the New York World and produced hundreds of tales of ordinary city people, famous for their warmth, wordplay and twist endings. He died in New York on 5 June 1910.
sections.historicalContext: Set in a cheap furnished flat in New York at the start of the twentieth century, when millions of clerks and shop workers lived on a few dollars a week. The title refers to the Magi of the Gospel of Matthew, who brought gifts to the infant Jesus, the origin of Christmas gift-giving.

publicationAndReception.publication: First published in the New York Sunday World on 10 December 1905; collected in The Four Million (1906), whose title answers the claim that only "four hundred" people in New York society mattered.
publicationAndReception.then: Immediately popular; it helped make O. Henry the best-known story writer in America.
publicationAndReception.now: One of the most adapted and anthologized Christmas stories, the classic example of situational irony and the "twist ending."

sections.overview: Della has one dollar and eighty-seven cents to buy her husband Jim a Christmas present. Each of them owns one treasure: her long hair and his gold watch.
sections.whyItMatters: Students learn how irony shapes meaning and think about what makes a gift valuable.

spoilerOverview.text: Della sells her hair to buy Jim a chain for his watch; Jim sells his watch to buy her combs for her hair. The narrator calls them the wisest of givers.

lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 6–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Gift of the Magi.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Gift of the Magi: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (sacrificial love, wealth and poverty, irony of giving) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Gift of the Magi teaches about sacrificial love. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how O. Henry develops sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how O. Henry develops sacrificial love across The Gift of the Magi. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Gift of the Magi (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of sacrificial love. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how O. Henry's choices in The Gift of the Magi (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of sacrificial love, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Gift of the Magi's treatment of sacrificial love in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on sacrificial love in The Gift of the Magi, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
